title: Large language models for intelligent RDF knowledge graph construction: results from medical ontology mapping
relevance_reason: The paper is primarily about LLM-based medical ontology mapping and RDF knowledge graph construction; ChromaDB vector database is mentioned only as a retrieval tool within the pipeline, with no analysis, comparison, or discussion of vector database technology itself.
research_focus: Comparative evaluation of six systems (five LLMs and one BERT-based method) for automated medical ontology mapping to SNOMED CT and RDF knowledge graph construction, using a combined quantitative and qualitative evaluation framework.
method: A data preprocessing pipeline (terminology normalization, abbreviation expansion, unit standardization) combined with an LLM-powered semantic mapping engine. A ChromaDB vector database populated with pre-computed BioBERT embeddings is used for efficient concept retrieval via cosine similarity. Six systems are compared using precision, recall, F-score, confusion matrix analysis, and qualitative expert assessment on a dataset of 108 medical terms.
mentioned_systems: ChromaDB; GPT-4o; Claude 3.5 Sonnet v2; Gemini 1.5 Pro; Llama 3.3 70B; DeepSeek R1; BERTMap; BioBERT
application_domain: Medical ontology mapping (SNOMED CT), RDF knowledge graph construction in healthcare
results_summary: The paper evaluated six systems for mapping 108 medical terms to the SNOMED CT ontology. GPT-4o achieved the highest performance with 93.75% precision, 98.90% recall, and 96.26% F-score, substantially outperforming all other systems. Gemini 1.5 Pro (F1 63.31%) and Claude 3.5 Sonnet v2 (F1 60.56%) ranked second and third, while Llama 3.3 70B (F1 30.16%) and DeepSeek R1 (F1 28.81%) showed the weakest performance. A chi-square test confirmed statistically significant differences between methods (p < 0.001, Cramer's V = 0.32). Error analysis showed that all systems struggled with complex quantitative measurements and multi-parameter clinical assessments, with GPT-4o's few errors concentrated in these areas.
limitations: Performance variability depends on training data quality and coverage, with rare or highly specialized concepts presenting challenges for all methods; The need for domain expert validation remains, particularly for critical applications; GPT-4o's high computational demands and cost may limit its feasibility for certain applications; The dataset of 108 medical terms, while expert-validated, is limited in size and may not fully capture generalizability; Complex quantitative measurements and multi-parameter clinical assessments remain challenging even for the best-performing system
research_gaps: Develop more efficient architectures that can match GPT-4o's performance while requiring fewer computational resources; Expand evaluation with a larger dataset covering more medical subfields and data formats to test scalability and adaptability; Explore models' performance with datasets involving more diverse relationships, temporal data, and hierarchical structures; Investigate hybrid approaches that combine symbolic reasoning with machine learning; Evaluate performance of different LLMs in niche areas of medical terminology mapping, especially in contexts with limited computational resources
